◑
One loop is all you need.

A guided tour of how a real coding agent harness is built — from a 30-line while True to a full multi-agent system — one mechanism per lecture, s01 → s20.

Agency comes from the model. An agent product = model + harness. The intelligence — the ability to perceive, reason, and act — is learned during training, not coded into the surrounding software. What we build is the harness: the environment that lets a trained model operate. The model decides; the harness executes. The model reasons; the harness supplies context, tools, permissions, memory, and teammates.

# The pattern that never changes — every lecture hangs off this:
while True:
    response = LLM(messages, tools)
    if not has_tool_use(response.content): return
    results = execute_tools(response.content)
    messages.append(results)

Claude Code's real complexity is not “a smarter agent brain.” It is the complexity of a mature harness built around that tiny loop. Each of the 20 lectures adds exactly one mechanism — and crucially, the loop itself barely changes. New capabilities attach around it: in the tool dispatch, before/after tool calls, before the LLM call, or in the message list.

The roadmap — six stages

Lectures below are in linear order (s01→s20, matching the course's “what's next” chain). These six stages group them by purpose. The colored dot on each sidebar item shows its stage.

1 · Let the agent act
s01 Agent Loop — one loop + bash
s02 Tool Use — one tool → many
s03 Permission — decide what can run
s04 Hooks — extension points
2 · Handle complex work
s05 TodoWrite — plan first
s06 Subagent — side work, clean context
s08 Context Compact — make room
3 · Remember & recover
s09 Memory — keep what matters
s10 System Prompt — assemble at runtime
s11 Error Recovery — retry or reroute
4 · Run long tasks
s12 Task System — persisted DAG
s13 Background Tasks — async work
s14 Cron Scheduler — fire on time
5 · Coordinate many agents
s15 Agent Teams — teammates + mailboxes
s16 Team Protocols — handshakes
s17 Autonomous Agents — self-claim
s18 Worktree Isolation — separate dirs
6 · Extend & assemble
s07 Skill Loading — knowledge on demand
s19 MCP Plugin — external tools
s20 Comprehensive — all of it, one loop
How to use this page: pick a depth at the top — Expanded lecture (teaching prose), Distillation (tight problem→solution→how), or Summary (bullets). Your choice applies to every module and is remembered. Each module shows its diagram and a key code snippet regardless of depth.
s01
The Agent Loop

“One loop & Bash is all you need.”

Stage 1 · Let the agent act
Harness layer: The Loop
The minimal runnable agent — under 30 lines.
EXPANDED LECTURE

Ask a chat model to “list my files and run build.py” and it will happily print a shell command — then stop. It won't execute it, and it won't reason about the output. You become the middle layer: run the command, paste the result back, wait for the next one. The agent loop automates exactly that round-trip.

The whole thing is a while True that hinges on one signal: did the model ask for a tool? If the response contains a tool call, the harness runs it, feeds the result back as a new message, and loops. If not, the model is done — exit. That's it. The model is the brain that decides; the loop is the body that acts and reports back.

Where it attaches: this is the loop. Every one of the next 19 lectures adds a mechanism somewhere around these five lines — in tool dispatch, before/after a tool, before the LLM call, or in the message list — but the skeleton never changes.

Pitfall: in real streaming responses, stop_reason can lag. Production Claude Code doesn't trust it — it checks whether a tool_use block is actually present. Same idea, more robust signal.
AGENT_LOOP — THE KERNEL
def agent_loop(messages):
    while True:
        response = client.messages.create(
            model=MODEL, system=SYSTEM, messages=messages,
            tools=TOOLS, max_tokens=8000)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return                          # model is done
        results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type == "tool_use":
                output = run_bash(block.input["command"])
                results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                    "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": output})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
messages
while True
stop_reason
tool_use

→ Next: s02 Tool Use — bash alone is clumsy — give the model 5 real tools.

s02
Tool Use

“Add a tool, add just one handler.”

Stage 1 · Let the agent act
Harness layer: Tool Dispatch
One tool (bash) becomes five via a dispatch map — the loop is untouched.
EXPANDED LECTURE

With only bash, the model has to spell out cat path to read, echo … > file to write, sed to edit. Every intent goes through a brittle layer of shell translation that wastes tokens and invites mistakes. The fix is to give the model purpose-built tools: read_file, write_file, edit_file, glob — plus bash.

Here's the elegant part: the loop from s01 doesn't change at all. The only edit is the one line that ran the tool. Instead of hardcoding run_bash(), we look the handler up in a dictionary: TOOL_HANDLERS[block.name](**block.input). Adding a tool is now two tiny steps — one entry in the TOOLS schema array (so the model knows it exists) and one entry in the dispatch dict (so the harness can run it).

Where it attaches: the dispatch map sits inside the tool-execution line of the loop. This indirection is the seam that every later tool — todo, task, skills, MCP — plugs into.

Concurrency note: the model often returns several tool calls at once. The teaching version runs them in order. Real Claude Code partitions them into batches: consecutive concurrency-safe calls (reads, globs, read-only bash) run in parallel; anything that mutates runs serially.
DISPATCH MAP
TOOL_HANDLERS = {
    "bash": run_bash, "read_file": run_read,
    "write_file": run_write, "edit_file": run_edit,
    "glob": run_glob,
}

# the only change to the s01 loop:
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        handler = TOOL_HANDLERS[block.name]   # lookup
        output  = handler(**block.input)       # call
        results.append({"type":"tool_result",
            "tool_use_id":block.id, "content":output})
TOOL_HANDLERS
dispatch map
tool schema
concurrency

→ Next: s03 Permission — bash can still run rm -rf / — add a gate before execution.

s03
Permission

“Set boundaries first, then grant freedom.”

Stage 1 · Let the agent act
Harness layer: Permission
Three gates before any tool runs: hard deny → rule match → ask the user.
EXPANDED LECTURE

Now the agent has five tools, and one of them — bash — is unrestricted. Tell it to “clean up the project” and it might run rm -rf /. Safety can't depend on trusting the model; it needs code that checks before every tool call.

The teaching design is a three-gate pipeline, evaluated in a fixed order. Gate 1 — hard deny: a blocklist of operations that never run (sudo, mkfs, rm -rf /). Gate 2 — rule match: context-dependent operations (writing outside the workspace, an rm on files) that need a closer look. Gate 3 — ask the user: when a rule matches, pause and ask for a yes/no. If no gate matches, the call just runs — that's the common path for routine reads and edits.

Where it attaches: a single check_permission(block) call inserted right before tool execution in the loop. One line.

Pitfall: string matching on commands is not real security — shell expansion and variants slip past it. It's a teaching stand-in. Real Claude Code has four outcomes (allow/deny/ask/passthrough), 8 rule sources merged by precedence, and an LLM-based classifier for auto-approval.
CHECK_PERMISSION — THREE GATES
def check_permission(block) -> bool:
    # Gate 1: hard deny list
    if block.name == "bash":
        if check_deny_list(block.input.get("command", "")):
            return False
    # Gate 2 + 3: rule match -> ask user
    reason = check_rules(block.name, block.input)
    if reason:
        if ask_user(block.name, block.input, reason) == "deny":
            return False
    return True
DENY_LIST
PERMISSION_RULES
allow/deny/ask
approval

→ Next: s04 Hooks — hardcoding checks in the loop bloats it — hang logic on hooks instead.

s04
Hooks

“Hook around the loop, never rewrite the loop.”

Stage 1 · Let the agent act
Harness layer: Hooks
Extension points fire around the loop; the loop only calls trigger_hooks().
EXPANDED LECTURE

Permission checks work — but every new cross-cutting concern (“log every bash call”, “git add after writes”, “warn on huge output”) tempts you to add another line inside the loop. Do that a few times and the loop becomes unreadable. You wanted to extend the agent's behavior, but you keep editing the core.

Hooks invert this. The loop becomes a stable kernel that only announces events; the behavior lives in callbacks registered against those events. Four events cover the full cycle: UserPromptSubmit (after input, before the LLM), PreToolUse (before a tool runs), PostToolUse (after), and Stop (about to exit). The s03 permission check is now simply a PreToolUse hook — moved out of the loop, not rewritten.

Where it attaches: the loop replaces its hardcoded check_permission() with trigger_hooks("PreToolUse", block); a non-None return means “block.” A Stop hook returning a value can even force the loop to continue.

Scale: teaching uses 4 events; real Claude Code defines 27 (sessions, subagents, compaction, teams…). All follow this same register/trigger pattern. A key production invariant: a hook returning allow still can't bypass deny/ask rules.
REGISTER / TRIGGER
HOOKS = {"UserPromptSubmit":[], "PreToolUse":[],
         "PostToolUse":[], "Stop":[]}

def trigger_hooks(event, *args):
    for cb in HOOKS[event]:
        result = cb(*args)
        if result is not None:   # non-None = stop/block
            return result
    return None

# in the loop, replacing the s03 hardcoded check:
blocked = trigger_hooks("PreToolUse", block)
if blocked:
    results.append(tool_result(block.id, str(blocked))); continue
register_hook
trigger_hooks
PreToolUse
Stop

→ Next: s05 TodoWrite — a safe agent still drifts on big tasks — give it a way to plan.

s05
TodoWrite

“An agent without a plan drifts.”

Stage 2 · Handle complex work
Harness layer: Planning
A planning tool that does no work — it just keeps the agent on course.
EXPANDED LECTURE

Give the agent a 10-step refactor and watch it lose the thread: it renames a few files, hits a test failure, fixes it, and by then the original goal has scrolled out of attention. The longer the conversation, the more tool output dilutes the plan. The agent improvises because steps 4–10 are no longer in view.

The cure is a todo_write tool that adds planning capability, not execution capability. It can't read files or run commands — it just records a checklist of steps with statuses (pending / in_progress / completed) kept in memory and printed to the terminal. Writing the plan down before acting, and updating it as it goes, keeps the goal anchored in recent context.

Where it attaches: nothing in dispatch changes — todo_write is just another entry in TOOL_HANDLERS. The one loop tweak is a small nag: if the model goes 3 rounds without touching its todos, inject a reminder.

Note: the “3-round nag” is a teaching device. Real Claude Code has no fixed round count; it nudges when several todos are all complete with no verification step. CC also runs two systems — lightweight TodoWrite and the file-backed Task System (that's s12).
RUN_TODO_WRITE
CURRENT_TODOS = []

def run_todo_write(todos):
    global CURRENT_TODOS
    CURRENT_TODOS = todos
    for t in todos:
        icon = {"pending":" ", "in_progress":"▸", "completed":"✓"}[t["status"]]
        print(f"  [{icon}] {t['content']}")
    return f"Updated {len(todos)} tasks"

# loop nag: 3 rounds without a todo -> remind
if rounds_since_todo >= 3:
    messages.append({"role":"user",
        "content":"<reminder>Update your todos.</reminder>"})
todo_write
pending/in_progress/completed
nag reminder

→ Next: s06 Subagent — some tasks are too big for one context — delegate to a clean one.

s06
Subagent

“Big tasks split small, each subtask gets clean context.”

Stage 2 · Handle complex work
Harness layer: Sub-Agent
A task tool spawns a fresh-context sub-agent and returns only the conclusion.
EXPANDED LECTURE

While fixing a bug the agent reads 30 files to trace a call chain, ballooning messages to 120 entries — most of them noise irrelevant to the fix. That noise crowds the context and makes the agent “forgetful.” When you debug, you'd open a scratch terminal, do the investigation, jot the answer, and return. The agent needs the same move.

The task tool spawns a sub-agent with a fresh messages[]. It runs its own loop, does the side quest, and returns only a summary string — all the intermediate steps are discarded. File-system side effects (writes, edits) persist in the working directory; the conversational clutter does not. The sub-agent gets a restricted toolset (no task, so it can't recurse) and still passes every call through the permission hooks — isolation of context is not isolation from security.

Where it attaches: task is one more handler in the dispatch map; the sub-agent reuses the same loop + hooks with its own message list and system prompt.

Real CC: three modes — fresh, fork (shares prompt cache for cheaper calls), and general-purpose — plus async background subagents. Recursion is guarded by a fork tag, not just “no task tool.”
SPAWN_SUBAGENT (CORE)
def spawn_subagent(description):
    messages = [{"role":"user", "content":description}]  # fresh!
    for _ in range(30):                                # safety cap
        response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL,
            system=SUB_SYSTEM, messages=messages,
            tools=sub_tools, max_tokens=8000)
        messages.append({"role":"assistant", "content":response.content})
        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use": break
        # ... run tools via hooks, append results ...
    return extract_text(messages[-1]["content"])     # only the conclusion
task
fresh messages[]
context isolation
no recursion

→ Next: s07 Skill Loading — different tasks need different knowledge — load it on demand, not upfront.

s07
Skill Loading

“Load knowledge on demand, not upfront.”

Stage 6 · Extend & assemble
Harness layer: Knowledge
A lightweight catalog in the prompt; full skill content fetched only when used.
EXPANDED LECTURE

Say your project has a React style guide, a SQL style guide, and an API design doc. The naive move is to concatenate all of them into the system prompt — and now every single LLM call, whether it's changing a CSS color or fixing a query, carries 6,000+ lines of mostly-irrelevant text. You're paying tokens to ship 99% noise on every turn.

Skills fix this with two levels. Level 1 is a tiny catalog — each skill's name + one-line description — scanned from a skills/ directory at startup and injected into the system prompt (~100 tokens each, carried every turn so the model knows what exists). Level 2 is the content: when the model decides it needs the SQL guide, it calls load_skill("sql-style") and the full SKILL.md arrives as a tool_result — paid for only when used. Lookups go through a registry, not raw paths, so there's no path-traversal risk.

Where it attaches: the catalog is part of the assembled system prompt (s10); load_skill is one more handler in the dispatch map. Crucially, skill content lands in messages, not the prompt — so it rides along in history until compaction (s08) drops it. On-demand loading answers “don't carry what you shouldn't”; compaction answers “how to drop what you should.”

Real CC loads skills from many sources (user/project/plugin/MCP/bundled), parses richer frontmatter (when_to_use, allowed-tools, context: fork), and budgets the catalog to ~1% of the context window.
TWO-LEVEL LOADING
def list_skills():                       # Level 1: catalog -> system prompt
    return "\n".join(f"- **{s['name']}**: {s['description']}"
                     for s in SKILL_REGISTRY.values())

def load_skill(name):                       # Level 2: full content on demand
    skill = SKILL_REGISTRY.get(name)
    if not skill: return f"Skill not found: {name}"
    return skill["content"]            # injected via tool_result, not the prompt
SKILL_REGISTRY
list_skills
load_skill
two-level loading

→ Next: s08 Context Compact — on-demand loading helps, but context still fills — learn to make room.

s08
Context Compact

“Context always fills up — have a way to make room.”

Stage 2 · Handle complex work
Harness layer: Compression
Four compaction layers — cheapest first, the LLM-summary nuke last.
EXPANDED LECTURE

An agent reads a 1000-line file, then 30 more, runs 20 commands — and every output piles into messages. The context window is finite; once it's full the API rejects the call with prompt_too_long. Without compaction, no agent can work on a large project for long.

The strategy is cheap first, expensive last — a pipeline run before each LLM call. L3 budget persists oversized tool results to disk, leaving a marker + preview. L1 snip trims the stale middle of the conversation (keep head + tail). L2 micro replaces all but the few most recent tool results with one-line placeholders. These three are pure text/structure work — zero API calls. Only if tokens still exceed the threshold does L4 compact spend one API call to LLM-summarize the whole history into a single message.

Where it attaches: the three preprocessors run at the top of each loop iteration (order matters — budget before micro, so big content is saved before it's placeholdered); L4 triggers on a token threshold; a reactive compact catches a prompt_too_long that slips through.

Order is load-bearing: L3 (budget) must run before L2 (micro) — otherwise micro replaces a huge result with a placeholder before its full content is saved to disk. A circuit breaker stops after 3 consecutive failures.
THE PIPELINE IN THE LOOP
while True:
    messages[:] = tool_result_budget(messages)   # L3 persist big results
    messages[:] = snip_compact(messages)          # L1 trim the middle
    messages[:] = micro_compact(messages)         # L2 placeholder old results
    if estimate_token_count(messages) > THRESHOLD:
        messages[:] = compact_history(messages)   # L4 LLM summary (1 call)
    try:
        response = client.messages.create(...)
    except PromptTooLongError:
        messages[:] = reactive_compact(messages)  # emergency
        continue
snip_compact
micro_compact
tool_result_budget
compact_history

→ Next: s09 Memory — compaction is lossy — keep a layer that survives it and the session.

s09
Memory

“Remember what matters, forget what doesn't.”

Stage 3 · Remember & recover
Harness layer: Memory
A file store + index that survives compaction and sessions — three subsystems.
EXPANDED LECTURE

Compaction (s08) preserves goals and open work, but it's lossy: “use tabs, not spaces” degrades to “has style preferences,” and a brand-new session starts with nothing. LLMs have no persistent state — everything lives in the context window, and the context window gets compressed. You need a layer that doesn't participate in compression and persists across sessions.

Memory is just files. Each memory is a small Markdown file with YAML frontmatter (name / description / type), and MEMORY.md is a one-line-per-memory index. Three subsystems work together: selection (at the start of a turn, an LLM side-query picks the few relevant memories to inject), extraction (when a turn ends, an LLM scans the dialogue for new preferences/constraints/facts and writes files), and consolidation (low-frequency dedup/merge once files pile up). Four types — user, feedback, project, reference — each answer a different question.

Where it attaches: the index goes into the system prompt (cacheable); selected file contents are injected on demand; extraction + consolidation fire in the loop's “turn ended” branch (stop_reason != tool_use).

Real CC selects with an LLM (not embeddings), runs extraction in a restricted forked agent, and gates consolidation (“Dream”) on time/session/lock — not a simple count.
EXTRACT + SELECT
# turn ended -> learn from the dialogue
if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
    extract_memories(messages)    # LLM finds new prefs/facts -> writes .md files
    consolidate_memories()        # dedup/merge when count >= threshold
    return

def select_relevant_memories(messages, max_items=5):
    catalog = build_catalog(list_memory_files())   # name + description
    indices = llm_pick(recent(messages), catalog)  # side-query
    return [files[i] for i in indices][:max_items]
MEMORY.md
selection
extraction
consolidation

→ Next: s10 System Prompt — the prompt is still a hardcoded string — assemble it at runtime.

s10
System Prompt

“Prompts are assembled at runtime, not hardcoded.”

Stage 3 · Remember & recover
Harness layer: Prompt
Sections assembled per-turn from real state, then cached.
EXPANDED LECTURE

From s01–s09 the system prompt was one hardcoded line. As capabilities grew, that string sprouted clauses — and three problems appeared: switching projects means rewriting the whole thing, one edit can break another, and every request carries every clause even when irrelevant.

The fix is to treat the prompt as configuration assembled at runtime. Split it into topic-keyed sections (identity, tools, workspace, memory). Some are always loaded; others load only when their real state is present — e.g. the memory section appears only if .memory/MEMORY.md exists. The decision is driven by actual state, never by keyword-sniffing the messages. A small cache (keyed by a deterministic serialization of the context) avoids re-assembling when nothing changed.

Where it attaches: at the top of each loop iteration, get_system_prompt(context) returns the assembled (or cached) prompt; update_context() refreshes the state after tools run.

Real CC has dozens of sections gated by flags/modes, a static/dynamic boundary for API-level prompt caching, and three cache layers. mcp_instructions is the one deliberately uncached section, since servers connect/disconnect between turns.
ASSEMBLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT
def assemble_system_prompt(context):
    sections = [PROMPT_SECTIONS["identity"],
                PROMPT_SECTIONS["tools"],
                PROMPT_SECTIONS["workspace"]]      # always
    if context.get("memories"):                  # on-demand, by real state
        sections.append(f"Relevant memories:\n{context['memories']}")
    return "\n\n".join(sections)

def get_system_prompt(context):
    key = json.dumps(context, sort_keys=True, default=str)
    if key == _last_key: return _last_prompt   # cache hit
    ...
PROMPT_SECTIONS
assemble_system_prompt
runtime state
cache key

→ Next: s11 Error Recovery — the agent still crashes on a 529 — make errors recoverable.

s11
Error Recovery

“Errors aren't the end, they're the start of a retry.”

Stage 3 · Remember & recover
Harness layer: Resilience
Classify the failure, pick a recovery path, then loop back and retry.
EXPANDED LECTURE

In production, API errors are normal, not exceptional. An agent that crashes on the first 529 overloaded is a car that stalls when you breathe on it. Three failure modes dominate: truncated output (ran out of max_tokens mid-sentence), context overflow (still too long after compaction), and transient failures (429 rate-limit / 529 overload).

Each gets a tailored recovery. Truncation: first escalate max_tokens 8K→64K and retry the same request; if still cut off, save the partial and inject a “resume mid-thought” prompt, up to 3 times. Overflow: trigger a reactive compact and retry once; if it's still too big, exit (compacting again won't help). Transient: exponential backoff + jitter (up to 10 tries), and after 3 consecutive 529s switch to a fallback model.

Where it attaches: wrap the LLM call in try/except + a with_retry helper; check stop_reason for truncation before appending; then continue to loop back. The loop body is otherwise untouched.

Real CC has a dozen-plus reason/transition codes (model errors, image errors, streaming aborts, stop-hook blocks, token-budget continuations, max-turns…), plus diminishing-returns detection that stops pointless continuations.
RECOVERY IN THE LOOP
try:
    response = with_retry(lambda: client.messages.create(
        model=state.current_model, messages=messages,
        tools=TOOLS, max_tokens=max_tokens), state)
except Exception as e:
    if is_prompt_too_long(e) and not state.compacted:
        messages[:] = reactive_compact(messages)
        state.compacted = True; continue
    return
if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens" and not state.escalated:
    max_tokens = 64000; state.escalated = True; continue
with_retry
backoff + jitter
max_tokens escalate
fallback model

→ Next: s12 Task System — one-shot tasks aren't enough — persist a dependency graph to disk.

s12
Task System

“Big goals break into small tasks, ordered, persisted to disk.”

Stage 4 · Run long tasks
Harness layer: Tasks
A file-backed task graph with dependencies — the base for multi-agent work.
EXPANDED LECTURE

A todo list (s05) is a session checklist; it has no ordering and vanishes when the session ends. But real projects have dependencies — you can't write the API before the schema exists, or tests before the API. You need a task system: each task is a JSON file on disk, tasks declare blockedBy dependencies forming a DAG, and progress survives across sessions.

Each Task has id, subject, description, status, owner, and blockedBy. Five tools manage them: create_task, list_tasks, get_task, claim_task, complete_task. The key guard is can_start() — a task is claimable only when every dependency is completed. Claiming sets an owner and flips pending → in_progress (preventing duplicate work later, with teammates); completing flips to completed and reports which downstream tasks it just unblocked.

Where it attaches: five more handlers in the dispatch map + a .tasks/ directory. The owner field and disk persistence are precisely what s15–s18 build multi-agent coordination on.

Real CC uses proper-lockfile for concurrent claims, a high-water-mark file so IDs are never reused, four separate task tools, and TaskCreated/TaskCompleted hooks. Claiming there resolves owner only; status is a separate update.
CLAIM & COMPLETE
def claim_task(task_id, owner="agent"):
    task = load_task(task_id)
    if task.status != "pending": return f"{task_id} is {task.status}"
    if not can_start(task_id):  return "Blocked by deps"
    task.owner, task.status = owner, "in_progress"
    save_task(task); return f"Claimed {task_id}"

def complete_task(task_id):
    task = load_task(task_id); task.status = "completed"; save_task(task)
    unblocked = [t.subject for t in list_tasks()
                 if t.status == "pending" and can_start(t.id)]
    return f"Completed; unblocked {unblocked}"

→ Next: s13 Background Tasks — slow commands block the loop — push them to the background.

s13
Background Tasks

“Slow ops go background, agent keeps thinking.”

Stage 4 · Run long tasks
Harness layer: Background
Slow work runs on a thread; completion is injected as a notification.
EXPANDED LECTURE

You don't stand and watch a washing machine for 30 minutes — you start it and go do other things. The agent's bash is no different: npm install takes minutes, and while it blocks, the agent sits idle (still billed by token). Fast ops (reads, git status) return instantly and need no special handling; slow ones do.

So slow commands move to a daemon thread. start_background_task returns a bg_id immediately, and the tool call gets a placeholder tool_result (“started, result later”) so the model knows it's running and can do other work. When the thread finishes, the result is collected and injected on a later turn as a <task_notification> — a fresh event, not reusing the original tool_use_id (the Messages API needs exactly one result per call). The model decides what's slow via a run_in_background param; a keyword heuristic is the fallback.

Where it attaches: tool execution forks into two paths (sync vs background); a collect step merges any ready notifications with this turn's results into one user message.

Real CC runs on a single-threaded event loop — “background” means “don't await,” redirecting output to files. It defines 7 background task types, a stall watchdog (detects stuck interactive prompts), and a priority notification queue.
START_BACKGROUND_TASK
def start_background_task(block):
    bg_id = next_bg_id()
    def worker():
        result = execute_tool(block)
        with background_lock:
            background_tasks[bg_id]["status"] = "completed"
            background_results[bg_id] = result
    background_tasks[bg_id] = {"command":block.input.get("command"), "status":"running"}
    threading.Thread(target=worker, daemon=True).start()
    return bg_id   # placeholder tool_result references this

→ Next: s14 Cron Scheduler — manual triggers only — give the agent an alarm clock.

s14
Cron Scheduler

“Fire on schedule, no human kick needed.”

Stage 4 · Run long tasks
Harness layer: Scheduling
A polling thread enqueues due jobs; an idle agent picks them up.
EXPANDED LECTURE

An alarm clock rings at 7:00 whether you're awake or not — no one has to watch it. Background tasks (s13) still need a human to kick them off. “Run tests at 9am,” “check CI every 30 minutes” — recurring work shouldn't need a person each time.

The design decouples producing work from executing it across four layers: a scheduler daemon thread polls once per second and checks each CronJob's 5-field cron expression; matches go into a queue; a queue processor notices the queue is non-empty and the agent is idle, and starts one turn; the agent loop consumes the queue and injects [Scheduled] … into messages. A date-aware minute marker prevents double-firing within a minute, and a per-job try/except keeps one bad job from killing the thread.

Where it attaches: two new daemon threads plus a cron_queue; the loop just drains the queue at the top. Jobs can be durable (written to .scheduled_tasks.json, restored on restart) or session-only.

Caveat: the scheduler lives inside the agent process — close the app and it stops. Durable only means the definition survives restart. For “run while the app is closed,” use system crontab/systemd. Real CC adds jitter (thundering-herd), auto-expiry, a 50-job cap, and a lock file for multi-session firing.
SCHEDULER THREAD
def cron_scheduler_loop():
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
        now = datetime.now()
        marker = now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
        for job in list(scheduled_jobs.values()):
            try:
                if cron_matches(job.cron, now) and _last_fired.get(job.id) != marker:
                    cron_queue.append(job)              # enqueue, don't run
                    _last_fired[job.id] = marker
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"[cron error] {job.id}: {e}")   # one bad job won't crash

→ Next: s15 Agent Teams — some jobs exceed one agent — spin up persistent teammates.

s15
Agent Teams

“Too big for one agent — delegate to teammates.”

Stage 5 · Coordinate many agents
Harness layer: Teams
Persistent teammate threads communicating through file-based inboxes.
EXPANDED LECTURE

“Refactor the entire backend” spans auth, the database layer, API routes, and tests — more than one agent's context can hold. s06's sub-agents are temps: called for one job, then gone. Here you need teammates that persist and can communicate while they work.

The mechanism is a MessageBus of file-based inboxes: each agent (the Lead and every teammate) has a .jsonl file; sending appends a line, reading consumes (read + delete). spawn_teammate launches a teammate in its own daemon thread with its own system prompt, message list, and a small toolset (bash/read/write/send_message) — running the same loop you've built. When a teammate finishes, it sends its summary to the Lead's inbox; the Lead injects inbox messages into its own history so its LLM can see and react.

Where it attaches: teammates are just more agent loops; the only new wiring is the inbox read/inject step after each Lead iteration. Files (not in-memory queues) are used because they're observable across threads.

Real CC writes directly to inbox files with proper-lockfile, defines 15 structured message types, runs teammates in tmux panes, and bubbles permission prompts up to the Lead's terminal via bidirectional polling.
MESSAGEBUS
class MessageBus:
    def send(self, frm, to, content, msg_type="message"):
        msg = {"from":frm, "to":to, "content":content,
               "type":msg_type, "ts":time.time()}
        with open(MAILBOX_DIR / f"{to}.jsonl", "a") as f:
            f.write(json.dumps(msg) + "\n")

    def read_inbox(self, agent):
        inbox = MAILBOX_DIR / f"{agent}.jsonl"
        if not inbox.exists(): return []
        msgs = [json.loads(l) for l in inbox.read_text().splitlines()]
        inbox.unlink(); return msgs   # consume: read + delete

→ Next: s16 Team Protocols — loose messages aren't enough — add structured handshakes.

s16
Team Protocols

“Teammates need shared communication rules.”

Stage 5 · Coordinate many agents
Harness layer: Protocols
Request → response, correlated by a shared request_id, with a small FSM.
EXPANDED LECTURE

s15's teammates can talk, but coordination is loose. Two situations expose the gap. Shutdown: killing a teammate's thread mid-write can leave half-written files — you want a handshake. Plan approval: a risky refactor should be reviewed before it runs. Both share one shape: one side sends a request, the other replies, and the two are linked by an ID, with a state machine tracking pending → approved/rejected.

So we add ProtocolState records keyed by a request_id, a dispatcher that routes inbox messages by type to handlers, and match_response that finds the request by id and validates the response type matches (a shutdown reply can't accidentally approve a plan). A unified consume_lead_inbox ensures protocol messages always update state before content is handled. Teammates also gain an idle loop: after a non-tool turn they wait on the inbox instead of exiting, so they can still answer a shutdown request.

Where it attaches: message routing sits on top of the s15 bus; the same single FSM serves both protocols. Adding a protocol = adding one branch.

Real CC splits shutdown into approved/rejected types, does three-way shutdown with system cleanup, validates messages with Zod schemas, and actually gates execution on approval — the teaching version demonstrates only the message flow.
MATCH_RESPONSE
def match_response(response_type, request_id, approve):
    state = pending_requests.get(request_id)
    if not state: return
    if state.type == "shutdown" and response_type != "shutdown_response":
        return                                  # type mismatch -> ignore
    if state.status != "pending": return      # already resolved
    state.status = "approved" if approve else "rejected"

→ Next: s17 Autonomous Agents — stop hand-assigning — let teammates claim work themselves.

s17
Autonomous Agents

“Teammates check the board, claim work themselves.”

Stage 5 · Coordinate many agents
Harness layer: Autonomy
Idle teammates poll the task board and self-claim — no Lead assignment.
EXPANDED LECTURE

In s16 the Lead still hands out every task — 10 tasks means 10 manual assignments. That doesn't scale. Teammates should watch the task board, claim unowned tasks whose dependencies are done, and look for the next one when they finish.

The teammate lifecycle grows a third phase: WORK → IDLE → SHUTDOWN. In IDLE, idle_poll checks every 5s — inbox first (protocol messages like shutdown take priority), then the board via scan_unclaimed_tasks (pending, no owner, all blockedBy complete). On a hit it auto-claims and returns to WORK; after a 60s dry spell it shuts down. Claiming checks the result rather than assuming success, so an already-owned task is skipped. After compaction may have shrunk its history, a teammate re-injects its identity.

Where it attaches: an outer WORK↔IDLE loop wraps the teammate's inner agent loop; the board is the same .tasks/ from s12. The Lead now only creates tasks and spawns teammates.

Real CC blends four mechanisms (idle notifications, 500ms mailbox polling, an fs.watch task watcher, active claiming) and guarantees claim atomicity with file locks — the teaching idle_poll folds these into one loop.
IDLE_POLL
def idle_poll(name, messages, role):
    for _ in range(IDLE_TIMEOUT // IDLE_POLL_INTERVAL):
        time.sleep(IDLE_POLL_INTERVAL)
        inbox = BUS.read_inbox(name)                  # ① inbox first
        if inbox:
            if any(m.get("type")=="shutdown_request" for m in inbox):
                return "shutdown"
            return "work"
        unclaimed = scan_unclaimed_tasks()            # ② then the board
        if unclaimed and "Claimed" in claim_task(unclaimed[0]["id"], name):
            return "work"
    return "timeout"
idle_poll
scan_unclaimed_tasks
auto-claim
WORK/IDLE/SHUTDOWN

→ Next: s18 Worktree Isolation — teammates clobber each other's files — give each its own directory.

s18
Worktree Isolation

“Each works in its own directory, no interference.”

Stage 5 · Coordinate many agents
Harness layer: Isolation
Git worktrees give each task an isolated directory + branch, bound by task id.
EXPANDED LECTURE

Alice and Bob now self-claim — but they work in the same directory. Both edit config.py and overwrite each other, with no clean way to tell whose change is whose. s15–s17 solved “who does what” and “how to communicate,” but not “where to work.”

git worktree is the answer: multiple working directories on one repo, each on its own branch. create_worktree makes .worktrees/<name> on branch wt/<name> and binds it to a task by writing the task's worktree field — without changing the task's status (so the Lead can pre-stage tasks+worktrees and let teammates claim them). When a teammate claims a worktree-bound task, its bash/read/write run with that directory as cwd. Cleanup is deliberate: keep_worktree preserves the branch for review; remove_worktree refuses by default if there are uncommitted changes. Every lifecycle event is appended to an audit log.

Where it attaches: three Lead tools + a per-teammate cwd context; the task's new worktree field ties goal (task) to place (directory).

Real CC has two paths: EnterWorktree (process.chdir for the current session) and AgentTool isolation (cwdOverride for sub-agents). It tracks worktree state in the session — there's no task↔worktree binding; the binding here is a teaching simplification.
CREATE_WORKTREE + CWD
def create_worktree(name, task_id=""):
    validate_worktree_name(name)                  # [A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}
    path = WORKTREES_DIR / name
    ok, _ = run_git(["worktree", "add", str(path), "-b", f"wt/{name}", "HEAD"])
    if task_id: bind_task_to_worktree(task_id, name)  # status unchanged
    return f"Worktree '{name}' at {path}"

def _run_bash(command):
    return run_bash(command, cwd=wt_ctx["path"])   # runs in the worktree

→ Next: s19 MCP Plugin — hand-written tools have limits — plug in external ones via MCP.

s19
MCP Plugin

“Not enough capability? Plug in more via MCP.”

Stage 6 · Extend & assemble
Harness layer: Plugins
Discover external tools over a standard protocol and merge them into the pool.
EXPANDED LECTURE

Every tool so far was hand-written. But you may already have services — a Jira API, an in-house deploy system, a Notion knowledge base — and you don't want to re-implement a tool for each. You need a standard protocol: implement it once on the service side, and the agent can call its tools regardless of language.

That's MCP (Model Context Protocol). An MCPClient connects to a server, discovers its tools (tools/list), and invokes them (tools/call). connect_mcp brings a server online; assemble_tool_pool then merges built-in tools with every connected server's tools, naming them mcp__<server>__<tool> to prevent collisions (all unsafe characters normalized to _). Because the tool pool now changes at runtime, the system-prompt cache from s10 is dropped — after connect_mcp the pool and prompt are rebuilt so the model can see and call the new tools.

Where it attaches: assemble_tool_pool() feeds the loop its tools/handlers each round; an MCP handler is just a thin closure over client.call_tool.

Real CC supports 6 transports (stdio/sse/http/ws/…), full OAuth, layered config precedence, reverse “channel” notifications from servers, and a structured permission system for MCP tools. The teaching version mocks servers in-process.
ASSEMBLE_TOOL_POOL
def assemble_tool_pool():
    tools = list(BUILTIN_TOOLS)
    handlers = dict(BUILTIN_HANDLERS)
    for server_name, client in mcp_clients.items():
        s = normalize_mcp_name(server_name)
        for tdef in client.tools:
            name = f"mcp__{s}__{normalize_mcp_name(tdef['name'])}"
            tools.append(prefixed_schema(tdef, name))
            handlers[name] = (lambda *, c=client, t=tdef["name"], **kw: c.call_tool(t, kw))
    return tools, handlers

→ Next: s20 Comprehensive — put all 19 mechanisms back into one running harness.

s20
Comprehensive Agent

“Many mechanisms, one loop.”

Stage 6 · Extend & assemble
Harness layer: Comprehensive
All 19 mechanisms placed around the same while True.
EXPANDED LECTURE

The first 19 lectures each add one mechanism in isolation — the right way to learn, but not how a real agent runs. A long-lived coding agent needs them all at once: tool dispatch and permission boundaries, hooks, todo + task graph, skills + memory + runtime prompt assembly, compaction + error recovery, background + cron, teams + protocols + autonomous claiming, worktree isolation, and MCP. The hard part isn't piling features up — it's seeing where each one sits around the loop.

And the punchline: the loop is still the same shape. Around it, in order, sit UserPromptSubmit hooks → cron/background notification injection → compaction → memory+skills+MCP assembling the system prompt → the LLM call (wrapped in recovery) → “is there a tool_use block?” → PreToolUse hooks + permission → tool/MCP/background dispatch → PostToolUse hooks → results (or task_notifications) back to messages → repeat; on no-tool, Stop hooks then return. Permission isn't hardcoded — it's a PreToolUse hook, so logging and audit attach at the same point.

Where it attaches: everywhere — and that's the lesson. Claude Code's complexity isn't a smarter brain; it's a complete harness wrapped around a tiny, unchanging loop.

27 built-in tools in the comprehensive build span bash/read/write/edit/glob, todo/task/skill/compact, the full task + cron + team + worktree + MCP toolsets — assembled fresh each round alongside any connected MCP tools.
THE SAME KERNEL, FULL HARNESS
while True:
    inject_cron_and_background(messages)      # s13/s14
    run_compaction_pipeline(messages)         # s08
    system = assemble_system_prompt(context)  # s07/s09/s10/s19
    tools, handlers = assemble_tool_pool()    # s02/s19
    response = with_recovery(call_llm)        # s11
    if not has_tool_use(response.content):
        trigger_hooks("Stop", messages); return   # s04
    results = execute_tools(response, handlers)  # s03 perm via PreToolUse hook
    messages.append({"role":"user", "content":results})

→ Next: The end is the beginning — your job is the harness, not the intelligence.

end
The end is the beginning

Many mechanisms, one loop.

From s01 to s20 the code grows more capable, but the kernel is unchanged. If you remember one thing: your job is the harness, not the intelligence. Build the environment — tools, knowledge, observation, action interfaces, permissions — well, and the model does the rest.

One loop. Twenty-four mechanisms.

A guided tour of how a real coding-agent harness is built — from a ~30-line while True to a production multi-agent runtime — explaining core.py and every session file s01 → s23.

Agency comes from the model; the product is model + harness. The intelligence — perceiving, reasoning, deciding — is learned during training. What this repository builds is the harness: the software environment that lets a trained model act. The model decides what to do; the harness executes it, supplies context, enforces permissions, remembers, and coordinates teammates.

# The kernel that never changes — every lecture hangs off this:
while True:
    response = client.messages.create(messages, tools=TOOLS)
    messages.append(assistant_message(response))
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use": return   # model is done
    results = dispatch_tools(response.content)            # act
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})  # observe

Claude Code's real complexity is not "a smarter brain." It is the complexity of a mature harness wrapped around that tiny loop. Each session adds exactly one mechanism — and the loop barely changes. New capabilities attach around it: in the tool dispatch, before/after a tool, before the model call, or in the message list.

The four principles of harness engineering
The model is the only source of decisions. The harness never branches on model output meaning — it only executes what the model requests.
Tools are the only interface to the world. Every action goes through a typed, schema-validated tool call.
Context is a managed resource. What the model sees each turn is curated, compressed, and injected deliberately.
Permissions are declarative, not procedural. What is allowed, blocked, or needs approval lives in configuration, not scattered through code.

def stream_loop(messages, tools, dispatch, system=None):
    while True:
        with client.messages.stream(model=MODEL, system=system or DEFAULT_SYSTEM,
                                     messages=messages, tools=tools, max_tokens=8000) as stream:
            for text in stream.text_stream: print(text, end="", flush=True)
            response = stream.get_final_message()
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return response
        results = dispatch_tools(response.content, dispatch)
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

Phase 1 · Core Agent Loop

Under 30 lines — this kernel is the heart of Claude Code; the rest is protection.
AGENT_LOOP — THE KERNEL
def agent_loop(messages, dispatch):
    while True:
        response = client.messages.create(
            model=MODEL, system=DEFAULT_SYSTEM, messages=messages,
            tools=BASIC_TOOLS, max_tokens=8000)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            break                                   # model produced a final answer
        results = dispatch_tools(response.content, dispatch)   # run requested tools
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})  # feed results back

def run_subagent(prompt):
    sub_messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]   # FRESH context
    while True:
        response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, system=SUBAGENT_SYSTEM,
                                          messages=sub_messages, tools=EXTENDED_TOOLS, max_tokens=8000)
        sub_messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":

        results = dispatch_tools(response.content, EXTENDED_DISPATCH)
        sub_messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

class AgentState(Enum):
    IDLE = "idle"; REQUESTING = "requesting"; WAITING = "waiting"; RESPONDING = "responding"

class ProtocolAgent:
    def handle(self, message):
        with self._lock:
            self.state = AgentState.RESPONDING        # atomic transition
        sub_history = [{"role": "user", "content": message}]
        while True:
            response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, system=self.system,
                                              messages=sub_history, tools=EXTENDED_TOOLS, max_tokens=4000)
            sub_history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
            if response.stop_reason != "tool_use": break
            sub_history.append({"role": "user", "content": dispatch_tools(response.content, EXTENDED_DISPATCH)})
        with self._lock:
            self.state = AgentState.IDLE
        return "".join(b.text for b in sub_history[-1]["content"] if hasattr(b, "text"))

def run_write(path, content):
    if os.path.exists(path):
        SNAPSHOTS[path] = open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").read()   # back up
    else:
        SNAPSHOTS[path] = None                          # marker: file is new
    open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8").write(content)
    return f"written: {path} (snapshot saved — use revert to undo)"

def run_revert(path):
    original = SNAPSHOTS.pop(path)
    if original is None:
        os.remove(path); return f"reverted: deleted {path} (it was new)"
    open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8").write(original); return f"reverted: {path}"

    @abstractmethod
    async def receive(self, agent_name, timeout=30.0): ...

class RedisMailbox(MailboxBackend):
    async def send(self, to_agent, message):
        await self._redis.publish(f"agent:{to_agent}:inbox", json.dumps(message))

async def initialize_mailbox():
    if HAS_REDIS:
        try:
            mb = RedisMailbox(REDIS_URL); await mb._redis.ping(); return mb
        except Exception:
            pass
    return QueueMailbox()              # transparent fallback — same API

Advanced Worktrees — Production Lifecycle

“Git state is sacred; every edge case handled.”

s23_worktree_advanced.py
Phase 6 · Enterprise Upgrades
SUMMARY
Guards: detached-HEAD refusal, dirty-tree warning, regex-sanitized names.
Stale pruning and finally-guaranteed teardown.
Conflict detection via pairwise file-diff intersection.
Concurrent asyncio.gather run → structured JSON report.
S23 — DETECT OVERLAPPING EDITS ACROSS BRANCHES
def analyze_parallel_conflicts(tasks):
    file_changes = {}
    for t in tasks:                                   # files each task branch touched
        rc, out, _ = _git(["diff", "--name-only", "HEAD", t.branch])
        if rc == 0 and out:
            file_changes[t.task_id] = set(out.splitlines())
    conflicts, ids = [], list(file_changes)
    for i in range(len(ids)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(ids)):
            overlap = file_changes[ids[i]] & file_changes[ids[j]]    # set intersection
            if overlap:
                conflicts.append(f"{ids[i]} <-> {ids[j]}: {', '.join(sorted(overlap)[:5])}")
    return conflicts

Claude Code analog: The production upgrade of s12 — full worktree lifecycle with safety checks and conflict detection.
Next → Conclusion — many mechanisms, one loop — and where to take it next.
end
Many mechanisms, one loop

The kernel from s01 is still running in s23.

From core.py through s23 the code grows enormously more capable, yet the central loop is unchanged: call the model, run what it asks for, feed results back. Everything else — planning, skills, compression, teams, permissions, hooks, sessions, caching, MCP, worktrees — attaches around that loop. If you remember one thing: your job is the harness, not the intelligence. Build the environment well, and the model does the rest.

Where to push it further
Parallel subagent spawning — dispatch several explore subagents with asyncio.gather, the way real Claude Code fans out.
Vector memory — replace the flat .agent_memory.md with a semantic store so only relevant memories are recalled.
Token/cost ledger — account spend per task and per tool type to find the expensive operations.
Webhook event bus — forward s16 lifecycle events to Slack / Datadog / PagerDuty without touching the loop.
LLM-as-judge evaluation — score outputs on accuracy, tool efficiency, and plan adherence to make the repo benchmarkable.

langchain-mcp-adapters
MCP 도구를 LangChain 에이전트에 연결하는 법 — 12개 강의
▸
소개

여러 MCP 서버 동시 사용 시 주의사항
12
전체 구조 요약
강의
강의
요약
핵심 개념만 빠르게 불릿으로.
◑
MCP 도구를, LangChain 에이전트에 그대로.

langchain-mcp-adapters는 MCP(Model Context Protocol) 서버의 도구를 LangChain/LangGraph 에이전트가 바로 쓸 수 있는 BaseTool로 변환해 주는 어댑터입니다. 이 강의는 그 사용법을 12단계로 나눠, 핵심 개념부터 실전 패턴까지 차근차근 익히도록 구성했습니다.

한 줄 요약 — 어댑터의 일은 "연결"과 "변환" 두 가지입니다. MCP 서버와의 연결(Transport)을 관리하고, 서버가 제공하는 Tool을 LangChain BaseTool로 바꿔 에이전트에 넘깁니다. 나머지(추론·도구 선택·응답)는 LLM과 LangGraph가 합니다.

# 이 가이드가 다루는 가장 작은 동작 단위
client = MultiServerMCPClient({ "서버이름": {…transport 설정…} })
tools = await client.get_tools() # MCP Tool → LangChain BaseTool
agent = create_react_agent(llm, tools) # 에이전트에 장착
await agent.ainvoke({ "messages": [("user", "질문")] })

모든 모듈은 이 흐름의 한 조각을 설명합니다. 연결 방식(Transport)을 고르고, 서버를 어떻게 실행할지 정하고, 세션을 어떻게 유지할지 결정하고, 에이전트에 붙여 스트리밍으로 답을 받는 — 그 전 과정입니다.

로드맵 — 6개 스테이지

아래 12개 모듈은 01→12 순서입니다. 6개 스테이지는 목적별 묶음이며, 사이드바의 색 점이 각 모듈의 스테이지를 나타냅니다.

01 개요 — 무엇을, 왜

3 · HTTP & 혼합

4 · 실행 모델 & 세션

5 · 에이전트 연동

이 페이지 사용법: 상단에서 깊이를 고르세요 — 강의(설명형 본문) 또는 요약(핵심 불릿). 선택은 모든 모듈에 적용되고 기억됩니다. 코드 예시와 표는 깊이와 무관하게 항상 표시됩니다. 오른쪽 위 ◑로 다크/라이트 테마를 바꿀 수 있습니다.
01
langchain-mcp-adapters 개요

“MCP 도구 → LangChain 도구로 자동 변환.”

1단계 · 기초
요약
역할: MCP Tool을 LangChain BaseTool로 변환 + 연결 관리.
진입점 2가지: 단일 서버 load_mcp_tools(session), 다중 서버 MultiServerMCPClient.
Transport는 stdio와 Streamable HTTP 두 종류.
설치: pip install langchain-mcp-adapters langchain-anthropic langgraph python-dotenv
주요 임포트 경로
# 단일 서버 — 세션 직접 관리
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client
from langchain_mcp_adapters.tools import load_mcp_tools

# 다중 서버 — 자동 세션 관리
from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient

# LangGraph 에이전트
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage
load_mcp_tools
MultiServerMCPClient
BaseTool
Transport

→ 다음: 02 Transport 비교 — 먼저 연결 방식을 골라야 한다 — stdio냐 HTTP냐.

02
Transport 비교: stdio vs Streamable HTTP

“로컬이면 stdio, 원격이면 HTTP.”

1단계 · 기초
요약
stdio: 클라이언트가 서버를 켜고 파이프로 통신. 로컬·보안·간단.
Streamable HTTP: 미리 떠 있는 서버에 연결. 원격·공유·인증.
판단 기준: 로컬 도구(npx/로컬 스크립트) → stdio, 팀 공유·클라우드 → HTTP.
핵심 차이 = 서버를 누가 켜는가.
두 방식의 설정 형태
# stdio — command/args로 서버를 직접 실행
{ "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "."],
  "transport": "stdio" }

# Streamable HTTP — 이미 떠 있는 서버 URL에 연결
{ "url": "http://localhost:8000/mcp",
  "transport": "streamable_http" }
stdio
streamable_http
SSE
로컬 IPC

→ 다음: 03 stdio 원리 — 왜 클라이언트가 서버를 직접 켜야만 할까?

03
stdio 원리 — 왜 클라이언트가 서버를 실행하나

“stdin/stdout 파이프는 부모-자식 프로세스에서만 연결된다.”

2단계 · stdio 심화
STDIO 통신 구조
클라이언트 프로세스
    │
    ├─ stdin  ──→  [MCP 서버 프로세스]  (JSON-RPC 요청 전송)
    └─ stdout ←──  [MCP 서버 프로세스]  (JSON-RPC 응답 수신)
요약
stdio 서버 = 포트 없음 · stdin 대기 · 단일 클라이언트 전용 프로세스.
stdin/stdout 파이프는 부모-자식 관계에서만 연결 → 클라이언트가 직접 실행해야 함.
stdio_client가 subprocess.Popen으로 서버를 띄우고 (read, write) 제공.
컨텍스트 종료 시 서버 프로세스 자동 종료.
내부 동작 — STDIO_CLIENT + CLIENTSESSION
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

server_params = StdioServerParameters(
    command="npx",
    args=["-y", "@upstash/context7-mcp@latest"],
)

# stdio_client가 내부적으로 subprocess.Popen으로 서버 실행
async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
    # read: 서버 stdout → 클라이언트 / write: 클라이언트 → 서버 stdin
    async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
        await session.initialize()        # MCP 핸드셰이크
        tools = await load_mcp_tools(session)
stdio_client
subprocess.Popen
ClientSession
initialize()

→ 다음: 04 서버 실행 4방식 — 서버가 어떻게 작성됐냐에 따라 command가 달라진다.

04
stdio 서버 실행 4방식 — command 설정

“서버 코드의 형태가 command/args를 결정한다.”

2단계 · stdio 심화
요약
npx: npm 공개 서버. ["-y", "패키지@latest", ...옵션].
uvx: PyPI 공개 서버. 이름이 다르면 --from 패키지 실행명.
uv run: 로컬 FastMCP server.py → mcp run으로 실행(if __name__ 불필요).
sys.executable: 현재 Python으로 스크립트 직접 실행(서버가 mcp.run() 호출).
네 가지 COMMAND/ARGS
# ① npx — Node.js 패키지
StdioServerParameters(command="npx",
    args=["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/allowed/path"])

# ② uvx — PyPI 패키지 (이름≠실행명이면 --from)
StdioServerParameters(command="uvx",
    args=["--from", "office-powerpoint-mcp-server", "ppt_mcp_server"])

# ③ uv run — 로컬 FastMCP server.py
StdioServerParameters(command="uv",
    args=["run", "--with", "mcp[cli]", "mcp", "run", MCP_SERVER_PATH])

# ④ sys.executable — 현재 Python으로 직접 실행
StdioServerParameters(command=sys.executable, args=[server_script],
    env={**os.environ, "TRANSPORT": "stdio"})
npx
uvx
uv run
sys.executable
FastMCP

→ 다음: 05 Streamable HTTP — 원격/공유 서버에 연결하는 방법.

05
Streamable HTTP 방식

“서버는 미리 떠 있어야 한다. 클라이언트는 연결만.”

3단계 · HTTP & 혼합
요약
설정: {"url": "...", "transport": "streamable_http"}.
인증: "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}.
서버는 미리 독립 실행 필요(mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", ...)).
직접 연결은 streamable_http_client(url) + ClientSession.
클라이언트 연결 + 인증 헤더
from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient

client = MultiServerMCPClient(
    {
        "secure_server": {
            "url": "https://api.example.com/mcp",
            "transport": "streamable_http",
            "headers": {
                "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_TOKEN",
                "X-API-Key": "your-key",
            },
        },
    }
)
tools = await client.get_tools()

# 서버 측: mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
streamable_http
url
headers
mcp.run(transport=...)

→ 다음: 06 stdio + HTTP 혼합 — 서버마다 다른 transport를 한 클라이언트에.

06
stdio + HTTP 혼합 사용

“로컬 도구와 원격 서비스를 한 에이전트에 모은다.”

3단계 · HTTP & 혼합
요약
한 MultiServerMCPClient에 stdio·HTTP 서버를 혼합 등록 가능.
get_tools() 한 번으로 모든 서버 도구를 통합 로드.
딕셔너리 키 = 서버 식별자 = 도구 이름 접두어.
로컬 프로세스 관리 + 원격 연결을 동시에 처리.
서버마다 다른 TRANSPORT
client = MultiServerMCPClient(
    {
        "filesystem": {                       # stdio — 로컬
            "command": "npx",
            "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/workspace"],
            "transport": "stdio",
        },
        "search": {                            # HTTP — 원격
            "url": "https://search-api.internal/mcp",
            "transport": "streamable_http",
            "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer token123"},
        },
    }
)
tools = await client.get_tools()
print(f"총 {len(tools)}개 도구 로드됨")
MultiServerMCPClient
혼합 transport
get_tools()
서버 키

→ 다음: 07 Sync vs Async — 이 라이브러리는 왜 전부 async인가?

07
Sync vs Async — async 전용 라이브러리

“MCP 통신은 I/O 바운드 → 모든 핵심 API가 async.”

4단계 · 실행 모델 & 세션
요약
핵심 API 전부 async: await get_tools(), async with stdio_client, ainvoke/astream.
이유: stdio·HTTP 통신은 I/O 바운드.
일반 스크립트 → asyncio.run(main()), Jupyter → await 직접.
실행 중 루프에서 asyncio.run() 재호출 금지(→ nest_asyncio 또는 전부 async).
환경별 실행
# 일반 Python 스크립트
import asyncio

async def main():
    client = MultiServerMCPClient({...})
    tools = await client.get_tools()
    ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

# Jupyter: 셀에서 직접 await (루프가 이미 실행 중)
tools = await client.get_tools()
async/await
asyncio.run
async with
nest_asyncio

→ 다음: 08 세션 관리 — 서버 상태가 있으면 세션을 유지해야 한다.

08
세션 관리 — Stateful vs Stateless

“서버에 상태가 있으면 세션을 살려 둬라.”

4단계 · 실행 모델 & 세션
요약
선택 기준 = 서버에 요청 간 상태가 있는가.
Stateful(async with 내내 유지): bash·outlook 등 상태 서버.
Stateless(요청마다 세션): fetch·search 등 무상태 서버.
다중 서버는 MultiServerMCPClient가 세션 자동 관리.
v0.1.0: async with MultiServerMCPClient 금지 → 인스턴스 생성 후 await get_tools().
장기 STATEFUL — 상태가 이어진다
async def main():
    async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            tools = await load_mcp_tools(session)
            agent = create_react_agent(ChatAnthropic(model=MODEL), tools)

            # 1) 작업 디렉터리 설정
            await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [("user", "작업 디렉터리를 /workspace로")]})
            # 2) 위 상태가 서버에 남아 있어 /workspace 기준으로 동작
            await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [("user", "현재 디렉터리에서 ls")]})
    # 블록 종료 → 세션 + 서버 프로세스 자동 정리

# ❌ v0.1.0+ 금지: async with MultiServerMCPClient(...) → NotImplementedError
Stateful
Stateless
ClientSession
NotImplementedError
lock 직렬화

→ 다음: 09 Agent 결합 — 가져온 도구를 에이전트에 붙인다.

09
LangChain Agent와 결합

“create_react_agent로 도구를 추론 루프에 넣는다.”

5단계 · 에이전트 연동
요약
권장: create_react_agent(llm, tools)(ReAct, 스트리밍·라우팅 제어 우수).
행동 지침: prompt=SystemMessage(content=...).
단순 케이스: langchain.agents.create_agent.
다중 서버 → System Prompt에 접두어별 라우팅 규칙 명시.
CREATE_REACT_AGENT + SYSTEM PROMPT
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage

llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-20250514")

agent = create_react_agent(
    llm,
    tools,
    prompt=SystemMessage(content="당신은 파일시스템 전문가입니다. 파일 관련 요청을 처리합니다."),
)

response = await agent.ainvoke(
    {"messages": [("user", "현재 디렉터리의 파일 목록을 보여줘")]}
)
print(response["messages"][-1].content)
create_react_agent
ReAct
SystemMessage
도구 라우팅

→ 다음: 10 실시간 스트리밍 — 답을 토큰 단위로 흘려보낸다.

10
AI 답변 실시간 스트리밍

“astream으로 토큰과 도구 호출을 실시간 표시.”

5단계 · 에이전트 연동
요약
astream(stream_mode="messages") + async for chunk, metadata.
chunk.content는 문자열 또는 블록 리스트(text + tool_use).
블록 type 분기: "text"→출력, "tool_use"→도구명 표시.
ToolMessage(도구 결과)는 보통 스킵(LLM이 처리).
스트리밍 처리 루프
async for chunk, metadata in agent.astream(
    {"messages": [("user", user_input)]},
    stream_mode="messages",
):
    if hasattr(chunk, "content") and chunk.content:
        if isinstance(chunk.content, str):
            print(chunk.content, end="", flush=True)
        elif isinstance(chunk.content, list):
            for block in chunk.content:
                if isinstance(block, dict):
                    if block.get("type") == "text":
                        print(block["text"], end="", flush=True)
                    elif block.get("type") == "tool_use":
                        print(f"\n[Tool: {block['name']}]", flush=True)
print("\n")

최소 동작 코드 (빠른 시작)
import asyncio
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent

async def main():
    load_dotenv()                       # ANTHROPIC_API_KEY 로드

    client = MultiServerMCPClient({
        "fetch": {
            "command": "uvx",
            "args": ["mcp-server-fetch"],
            "transport": "stdio",
        },
    })
    tools = await client.get_tools()

    agent = create_react_agent(ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-20250514"), tools)
    response = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [("user", "https://example.com 내용을 가져와줘")]})
    print(response["messages"][-1].content)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

01부터 12까지, 결국 반복되는 것은 하나입니다 — MCP 서버에 연결해 도구를 가져오고(get_tools), 에이전트에 붙여(create_react_agent) 호출한다(ainvoke/astream). Transport·세션·라우팅은 모두 이 한 줄을 안정적으로 굴리기 위한 주변 장치입니다. 서버의 상태 유무를 보고 세션 전략을 고르고, 서버 키로 도구 이름을 네임스페이싱하고, System Prompt로 라우팅을 알려 주면 — 나머지는 모델이 합니다.
